rv.q: I can’t see anything other than A*s being bestowed on Walker’s unmissable performance...School-days may or may not be the best days of our lives; what this riveting evening brings home is how crucial they invariably are.
Dominic Cooke’s production rewires the drama so that its historical importance is shown, its autobiographical element made vivid, its currency made vivacious.
This is a play about art, education and defying a society rigged against you.
A bright, humane entertainment, and rather humbling, too, especially if you've ever taken your education for granted.
Ultimately though, Cooke’s production is a rejuvenation.
But if it is comfort viewing, it is undeniably artful, affecting and hugely entertaining.
The greatest strength here is that he finds the play’s missing heart.
Around Walker, a delectable world is built.

Yes, it’s all very old-fashioned, and the neatly packaged ending wouldn’t get through a script conference at Call the Midwife. Signing off with Thanks for the Memory is clumsy, too. Yet for all that, it’s still a curiously watchable time capsule.
Walker provides a compelling argument for the time-honoured appeal of an inspirational teacher.
It is all perfectly watchable, if slow.
Strong performances and an undeniable momentum make it fun to watch, but there's not much to ponder when the music fades.
But I'm not sure Emlyn Williams's 1938 autobiographical homage to his overbearing school teacher makes the best use of her talents.
It is a triumph, an evening full of humour, feeling and inspiration.
And at its zenith, education should be life-changing – a great leveller in a meritocratic society.
The audience positively purred with pleasure throughout the two and half hours playing time which flew by.
At the centre is Nicola Walker’s Miss Moffat.
In Cooke’s production, told in the most sophisticated way.
The framing device both adds to the original play, while also dare I say improving it, and at the same time draws attention to the shortcomings of Williams’s writing.
This is not a great play and it’s presented as a larky excuse to mock stereotypes that died out 70 years ago.
It’s heartwarming, yes, and a superb story that never fades because its aspirations, like the corn, stay green.
DOMINIC Cooke’s buoyant production of Emlyn Williams’ play is unashamedly feel-good theatre.
Dominic Cooke refreshes this Pygmalion meets Dead Poets Society tale with an entertaining metatheatrical spin...

cn.t: Cooke's imaginative revival breathes new life into Williams' 1938 play, with Walker delivering a powerhouse performance as the inspirational teacher. Critics mostly praise its artful, entertaining execution, though some find it dated or overly sentimental.
